title: The error is perpendicular
objectives: Show that the projection error is orthogonal to the space.
Use Pythagoras to explain why the projection is the closest point.

screens.prose: The line runs along $\mathbf{a} = (2, 1)$, and $\mathbf{p} = (2, 1)$ is the projection of $\mathbf{b} = (1, 3)$. Drag P anywhere on the line. The caption shows two squared distances.
screens.question: What is $|\mathbf{b} - P|^2 - |P - \mathbf{p}|^2$, wherever P is?

options.why: At P = (5, 2.5) the caption reads 16.25 and 11.25. The first is always bigger.
Try P = (0, 0) and P = (4, 2). Both give 10 − 5 = 5.
10 is $|\mathbf{b} - P|^2$ at P = (0, 0) alone. Subtract $|P - \mathbf{p}|^2 = 5$ there.

hints.text: Subtract the two numbers in the caption at three different places.

feedback.correct: The gap is always 5, which is $|\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p}|^2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the second number in the caption from the first, at several places.

explain.text: The gap is always $5 = |\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p}|^2$, so $|\mathbf{b} - P|^2 = |\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p}|^2 + |P - \mathbf{p}|^2$. That is Pythagoras, with the right angle at $\mathbf{p}$. Any $P \neq \mathbf{p}$ adds a positive amount, so $\mathbf{p}$ is the closest point.

screens.title: Where the right angle is
screens.prose: The segment from $\mathbf{p}$ to $\mathbf{b}$ is the error $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p} = (-1, 2)$. The sum you found, $|\mathbf{b} - P|^2 = |\mathbf{e}|^2 + |P - \mathbf{p}|^2$, is Pythagoras on the triangle $\mathbf{b}$, $\mathbf{p}$, P.
screens.question: Why does Pythagoras hold for every P on the line?

options.text: $P - \mathbf{p}$ lies along the line, and $\mathbf{e}$ is perpendicular to the line

options.why: $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 2 + 3 = 5$, not 0. The right angle is at $\mathbf{p}$, not at the origin.
At P = (6, 3), $|\mathbf{e}|^2 = 5$ but $|P - \mathbf{p}|^2 = 20$. Pythagoras needs a right angle, not equal sides.
The gap was 5 at every P you dragged to, not only at the origin.

hints.text: Pythagoras needs a right angle between two sides of the triangle.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{e} \cdot (P - \mathbf{p}) = 0$ for every P on the line.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the right angle in the triangle, and say which two sides meet there.

explain.text: $P - \mathbf{p}$ is a multiple of $\mathbf{a}$, and $\mathbf{e} \cdot \mathbf{a} = -2 + 2 = 0$. So the triangle has its right angle at $\mathbf{p}$ whatever P is. This is why the projection is the closest point.

screens.title: In three dimensions
screens.prose: Now a plane in 3D: the column space of $\mathbf{A}$, with columns $(1, 1, 1)$ and $(0, 1, 2)$. Last lesson $\mathbf{b} = (6, 0, 0)$ projected to $\mathbf{p} = (5, 2, -1)$.
screens.question: Find $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p}$, then $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{e}$.

hints.text: Each row of $\mathbf{A}^T$ is a column of $\mathbf{A}$. Dot each with $\mathbf{e} = (1, -2, 1)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract $\mathbf{p}$ from $\mathbf{b}$, then dot $\mathbf{e}$ with each row of $\mathbf{A}^T$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$ says $\mathbf{e}$ is perpendicular to both columns, so to the whole plane $C(\mathbf{A})$. In the language of the four subspaces, $\mathbf{e}$ lies in $N(\mathbf{A}^T)$, the left nullspace.

screens.prose: $\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{A}(1, 1) = (1, 2, 3)$ is another point of the plane. Pythagoras says it is further from $\mathbf{b}$ than $\mathbf{p}$ is.
screens.question: Compute $|\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{q}|^2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract $\mathbf{q}$ from $\mathbf{b}$, then square each entry and add.

byKey.pq: 32 is $|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}|^2$. You want the distance from $\mathbf{b}$.
byKey.root: That is the distance. The question asks for its square.

explain.text: $|\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{q}|^2 = 38$, while $|\mathbf{e}|^2 = 1 + 4 + 1 = 6$ and $|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}|^2 = |(4, 0, -4)|^2 = 32$. So $38 = 6 + 32$: Pythagoras again. $\mathbf{q}$ is $\sqrt{38}$ from $\mathbf{b}$, $\mathbf{p}$ only $\sqrt{6}$.

screens.prose: Same plane, but now $\mathbf{b} = (1, -2, 1)$, the old error itself.
screens.question: What is the projection $\mathbf{p}$ of this $\mathbf{b}$?

options.why: That needs $\mathbf{b}$ in the plane. Here $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}$: $\mathbf{b}$ is perpendicular to it.
$\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}$ makes $\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{0}$, so no column is used.
Projection does not shrink $\mathbf{b}$ towards itself. It lands in the plane, and $\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{b}$ is not in it.

explain.text: A $\mathbf{b}$ perpendicular to the plane projects to $\mathbf{0}$: all of it is error. At the other extreme, $\mathbf{b} = (1, 2, 3)$ lies in the plane, so $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$. Every other $\mathbf{b}$ splits between the two.

screens.prose: Back to the picture in 2D: $\mathbf{b} = (1, 3)$, its projection $\mathbf{p} = (2, 1)$ and the error $\mathbf{e} = (-1, 2)$, drawn from $\mathbf{p}$.
screens.question: Which of these dot products is 0?

options.why: $\mathbf{e} \cdot \mathbf{b} = -1 + 6 = 5$. The error is not perpendicular to $\mathbf{b}$.
$\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{a} = 2 + 3 = 5$. If it were 0, $\mathbf{p}$ would be $\mathbf{0}$.
$\mathbf{e} \cdot \mathbf{e} = |\mathbf{e}|^2 = 5$. Only the zero vector has $\mathbf{e} \cdot \mathbf{e} = 0$.

hints.text: The right angle is drawn where the error meets the line.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{e} \cdot \mathbf{a} = -2 + 2 = 0$: the error is perpendicular to the space.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute each dot product, or look for the right-angle mark.

byKey.eb: You assumed the error is perpendicular to $\mathbf{b}$. It is perpendicular to the line: $\mathbf{e} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 5$ but $\mathbf{e} \cdot \mathbf{a} = 0$.

explain.text: The right angle sits at $\mathbf{p}$, between $\mathbf{e}$ and the line, not at the origin. In fact $\mathbf{e} \cdot \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{e} \cdot (\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{e}) = 0 + |\mathbf{e}|^2 = 5$. The error is perpendicular to $\mathbf{b}$ only when $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$.

screens.prose: Now the proof for any $\mathbf{A}$ with independent columns. Take $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ with $\hat{\mathbf{x}} = (\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{b}$, and $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p}$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the proof in order.

lines.text: $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{b}$, since a matrix times its inverse is $\mathbf{I}$
$(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}) \cdot \mathbf{e} = \mathbf{y}^T\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{e} = 0$ for every $\mathbf{y}$, so $\mathbf{e}$ is perpendicular to all of $C(\mathbf{A})$
For any $\mathbf{q}$ in $C(\mathbf{A})$, $\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{q} = \mathbf{e} + (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q})$, and $\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}$ is in $C(\mathbf{A})$

hints.text: The last line is the Pythagoras you saw on the line, now in any dimension.
Simplify A-transpose p, subtract, extend to the whole space, split b − q, expand.

feedback.correct: Equality holds only when $\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{p}$, so $\mathbf{p}$ is the unique closest point.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Prove $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$ first, then compare $\mathbf{b}$ with any other point $\mathbf{q}$.

byKey.c3: Perpendicular to all of $C(\mathbf{A})$ follows from $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$, so that comes first.

explain.text: The first three lines show the error is perpendicular to the whole space. The last two turn that into Pythagoras: every other point of $C(\mathbf{A})$ adds $|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}|^2 > 0$. That is why projection solves least squares.

screens.title: Residuals of a regression
screens.prose: A regression of a stock's daily returns on an intercept and the market gives the fit $0.1 + 1.2m$. The design matrix has columns $\mathbf{1} = (1, 1, 1, 1)$ and $\mathbf{m}$. The residuals are the error $\mathbf{e}$.
screens.question: Fill in the residuals, their sum, and $\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{e}$.

hints.text: Residual = stock return − fitted return, day by day.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the fitted return from the stock's return, then add, then dot with the market.

explain.text: The sum is $\mathbf{1} \cdot \mathbf{e} = 0$ because the intercept column is in $\mathbf{A}$. And $\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{e} = 0$ because $\mathbf{m}$ is too. With mean-zero residuals, $\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{e} = 0$ means the residuals are uncorrelated with the market.

screens.prose: A colleague fits a stock's returns by eye: $0.1 + 0.9m$. Its residuals sum to 0, but they rise with the market: $\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{e} > 0$.
screens.question: What does the positive $\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{e}$ tell you?

options.text: The fit is not least squares: a larger beta would shrink the squared errors
The stock has a positive alpha
options.why: Alpha is the intercept, and the residuals already sum to 0. $\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{e}$ is about the slope.

options.text: Nothing: residuals always correlate with the market
options.why: Least squares residuals are perpendicular to every column, so $\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{e} = 0$ exactly.
Residuals that rise with $m$ mean the fit is too flat. More of the stock moves with the market than 0.9 allows.

hints.text: For the least squares fit, the error is perpendicular to every column.
$\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{e} > 0$ means part of $\mathbf{e}$ still points along $\mathbf{m}$.

feedback.correct: Part of the error still lies along $\mathbf{m}$, so the fit has not projected it away.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what $\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{e}$ is for the least squares fit.

explain.text: Least squares leaves no part of $\mathbf{e}$ along any regressor. A positive $\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{e}$ means some of the error lies along $\mathbf{m}$. Moving it into the fit raises beta and lowers $|\mathbf{e}|^2$, by Pythagoras.

ideas: The error $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p}$ satisfies $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$: it lies in $N(\mathbf{A}^T)$, perpendicular to $C(\mathbf{A})$.
For any other $\mathbf{q}$ in the space, $|\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{q}|^2 = |\mathbf{e}|^2 + |\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}|^2$, so $\mathbf{p}$ is the closest point.
Regression residuals are perpendicular to every regressor: they sum to zero with an intercept and are uncorrelated with each regressor.

formula.name: The error is perpendicular
formula.note: If $\mathbf{b}$ is in $C(\mathbf{A})$, $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$. If $\mathbf{b}$ is perpendicular to it, $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{0}$.

summary.trap: The error is perpendicular to the space, not to $\mathbf{b}$: $\mathbf{e} \cdot \mathbf{b} = |\mathbf{e}|^2$.

options.why: That is $\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{b}$. The error is $\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p}$.
That is $\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}$. Subtract the projection $3\mathbf{a}$, not $\mathbf{a}$.
That subtracts $9\mathbf{a}$: you forgot to divide $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 9$ by $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a} = 3$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $\mathbf{p}$ first, then $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p}$.

quiz.prose: A vector $\mathbf{b}$ has length 10. Its projection onto a subspace has length 8.
quiz.question: How long is the error?

byKey.sub: Lengths do not subtract; squares do. $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{e}$ are at right angles.

explain.text: $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{e}$ are perpendicular and add to $\mathbf{b}$. So $|\mathbf{b}|^2 = |\mathbf{p}|^2 + |\mathbf{e}|^2$, giving $|\mathbf{e}| = \sqrt{100 - 64} = 6$.

quiz.prose: $\mathbf{p}$ is the projection of $\mathbf{b}$ onto $C(\mathbf{A})$, and $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p} \neq \mathbf{0}$.
quiz.question: Which statement is always true?

options.why: $\mathbf{e} \cdot \mathbf{b} = |\mathbf{e}|^2$, which is positive when $\mathbf{e} \neq \mathbf{0}$.
It is $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$: the rows of $\mathbf{A}^T$ are the columns of $\mathbf{A}$.
$|\mathbf{p}|^2 = |\mathbf{b}|^2 - |\mathbf{e}|^2$, which is smaller.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{p}$ is in $C(\mathbf{A})$, and $\mathbf{e}$ is perpendicular to all of it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. $\mathbf{e}$ is perpendicular to every vector in $C(\mathbf{A})$. Which vector listed is in it?

explain.text: $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ is in the column space, so $\mathbf{e} \cdot \mathbf{p} = \hat{\mathbf{x}}^T\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{e} = 0$. The error is not perpendicular to $\mathbf{b}$ itself.

quiz.prose: A regression on an intercept and the market leaves residuals 0.3, −0.1, $r$ and 0.2 (in %).
quiz.question: What is $r$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With an intercept column, the residuals sum to 0.

byKey.zero: A single residual need not be 0. Their sum is.

explain.text: The intercept column $\mathbf{1}$ is in $\mathbf{A}$, so $\mathbf{1} \cdot \mathbf{e} = 0$. The other three sum to 0.4, so $r = -0.4$.
